translations.text: The Book of Ruth.

In the days of the judges, there was a famine in the land. A man went from Bethlehem in Judah to live in the land of Moab, along with his wife and his sons, because the famine had become severe in the land.
The man's name was Elimelech, his wife's name was Naomi, and his sons' names were Mahlon and Chilion. They were Ephrathites from Bethlehem in Judah. They came to the land of Moab to live there.
Elimelech, Naomi's husband, died, and she was left with her two sons.
They married Moabite women. One was named Orpah, and the other was named Ruth. They lived there for about ten years.
Both her sons, Mahlon and Chilion, died, and the woman was bereaved of her husband and both her sons.
She and the two women set out to return from the land of Moab, because they had heard in the land of Moab that the Lord had visited his people to give them food.
She left the land where they had been living, with her two daughters-in-law accompanying her, to return to the land of Judah.
Naomi said to her daughters-in-law, “Go back to your own country and your families' homes. May the Lord show you kindness, just as you have shown kindness to me and to both my sons who died.
May the Lord grant you mercy, and may you find rest in your fathers' homes.” She kissed them, and they raised their voices and wept.
They said to her, "No! We will go with you to your land and your people."
Naomi said to them, “Go back, my daughters. Why are you going with me? Could I have sons again and give them to you as husbands?
Go back, my daughters, because I am too old to marry. Even if I said that I still had hope, and married and bore sons,

would you wait for them until they grew up, and hold back from marrying? No, my daughters. I am deeply embittered on your account, and it is more bitter for me than for you, because the Lord's hand has gone out against me.”
They raised their voices again and wept. Orpah kissed her mother-in-law, turned back, and left, but Ruth stayed with her.
Her mother-in-law said to her, “Look, your sister-in-law has gone back to her people and her family's home. You too should go back after your sister-in-law.”
Ruth said to her, “Far be it from me to turn back from you and leave you! Wherever you go, I will go, and wherever you live, I will live. Your people are my people, and your God is my God.
Where you die, I too will die and be buried. May God do so to me, and more besides, if anything but death alone separates me from you.”
When Naomi saw that she was firmly determined to go with her, she stopped telling her to leave.
They came together to Bethlehem in Judah. When they arrived in Bethlehem, the whole town rejoiced over them, and people said, “This is Naomi!”
She said to them, “Do not call me Naomi. Instead, call me ‘Bitter in spirit,’ because God Almighty has made me very bitter. For I went away from here full,
but the Lord has brought me back empty. Why, then, do you call me Naomi, when the Lord has humbled me, and the one who has the power has brought harm on me?”
Naomi returned with Ruth the Moabite, her daughter-in-law, who had wholeheartedly chosen to return with her. They came from the land of Moab at the beginning of the barley harvest.
Naomi had a certain acquaintance from the family of her husband Abimelech, a well-known man named Boaz.

Ruth the Moabite said to Naomi, her mother-in-law, “Let me go to the field and gather the leftover grain behind the workers of someone who looks kindly on me.” Her mother-in-law said to her, “Go, my daughter.”
Ruth went to gather the leftover grain behind the reapers, and she happened upon the portion of the field belonging to Boaz, who was from Abimelech's family.
Just then Boaz came from Bethlehem and said to the reapers, “Peace be with you.” They said to him, “May the Lord bless you.”
Boaz said to the young man in charge of the workers, “What can you tell me about this young woman?”
The young man answered him, “She is a Moabite woman, the one who came with Naomi from the land of Moab.”
She said, ‘Let me gather the leftover grain behind the reapers.’ She has been gleaning from morning until the rest periods.”
Boaz said to Ruth, “My daughter, have you not heard the proverb, ‘Do not glean in a field that is not yours’? Therefore stay, and spend the night here with my young women.”
“Watch where they are harvesting, and follow them. Look, I have instructed the young men that no one is to rebuke you. If you become thirsty, go and drink from the vessels that the young men fill.”
She fell facedown on the ground, bowed before him, and said, “Why have I found favor in your eyes, so that you take notice of me, though I am a foreigner?”

Boaz said to her, “I have been fully told what you have done for your mother-in-law since your husband died: how you left your father, your mother, and your family, and came to a people you had not known before.”
“May the Lord, the God of Israel, repay you and give you your reward, since you have come to take shelter under his wings.”
She said to him, “For I have found favor in your eyes, my lord, and you have comforted me and spoken to the heart of your servant. I will be like one of your servant women.”

At mealtime Boaz said to her, “Come here and eat bread with me.” He seated her beside the harvesters and gave her roasted grain meal. “Dip your bread in the vinegar.” He set out portions of roasted grain and gave them to her. She ate, was satisfied, and had some left over.
She got up to glean, and Boaz instructed his servants, saying, “Let her glean among the sheaves, and do not rebuke her.”
They let her glean among the sheaves.
They did not rebuke her. She gleaned in the field until evening, then beat out what she had gathered and found that it amounted to about a full measure of barley.
She picked it up and went into the town. She showed her mother-in-law what she had gleaned, and gave her some of what she had left over from her meal.

Her mother-in-law said to her, “Where were you gleaning today? Blessed be the place where you were, and the man in whose eyes you found favor!” She told her mother-in-law where she had been, saying, “The name of the man in whose field I was gleaning today is Boaz.”

Naomi said to her daughter-in-law, “Blessed is the Lord, who has not withdrawn his kindness from the living or the dead.” Naomi said to her, “The man is our relative, and he is one of those entitled to redeem our inheritance.”
Ruth said to her mother-in-law, “He also told me, ‘Stay close to my servants until the entire harvest is finished.’”
Naomi said to Ruth her daughter-in-law, “How fortunate you are, my daughter, that you stayed close to his young women, so that no one would rebuke you in a field you did not know.”
But you stayed close to Boaz’s servant women to glean until the barley and wheat harvest was finished. Ruth lived with her mother-in-law.
Naomi said to her, “My daughter, should I not seek a place of rest for you, so that things may go well for you?
“Now Boaz, [?], is the one whose young women you were with. Look, tonight he is winnowing barley on the threshing floors.”
“So wash, anoint yourself, dress in your clothes, and go down to the threshing floor. Do not let him see you until he has eaten and drunk.”
“When he lies down, take note of the place where he lies. Then go over and lie down at his feet, and he will tell you what to do.”
She said to her, “I will do everything you have told me.”
She went down to the threshing floors and did everything her mother-in-law had instructed her to do.

When Boaz had eaten and drunk and was feeling cheerful, he went and lay down at the side of the threshing floor. While he lay there, enjoying a sweet sleep, she came quietly, uncovered the edge of his cloak, and lay down at his feet.
In the middle of the night the man stirred from his sleep and was astonished to see a woman lying at his feet.
He said to her, “What is your news?” She said to him, “I am Ruth, your servant. Cover your servant with the edge of your cloak, for you are the one entitled to redeem the inheritance.”
Boaz said to her, “May God bless you, my daughter. You have made this last act of kindness much greater than the first, because you have not gone after young men, whether rich or poor.”
“Now, my daughter, do not be afraid. I will do for you everything you ask of me, for the whole community of our people knows that you are a woman of strength.”
“Now, it is true that I am entitled to redeem the inheritance. However, there is another who is entitled to redeem it, and he is a closer relative than I am.”

“Now stay here today, and spend the night until dawn. In the morning, if he will redeem you, good; let him do so. But if he is unwilling to redeem you—as the Lord lives, if he does not redeem you, I will redeem you.” He said to her, “Lie down until morning.”

She lay at his feet until dawn and got up in the morning while it was still dark, before anyone could recognize another person. She said to him, “Let no one know that I came down to you at the threshing floor.”
Boaz said to her, “Spread out your cloak.” She spread it out, and he measured out six measures of barley for her and loaded it onto her. She took it and went into the town.
She went in to her mother-in-law. Her mother-in-law said to her, “Who are you, my daughter?” She said to her, “It is I, Ruth.” And she told her everything Boaz had done for her.
She also told her that he had given her six measures of barley and had said to her, “Do not go to your mother-in-law empty-handed.”
Her mother-in-law said to her, “Stay here, my daughter, until you see what happens, for the man will not rest until he settles the matter today.”

Boaz went up and sat at the town gate. Just then the kinsman entitled to redeem the inheritance, whom Boaz had mentioned, passed by. He said to him, “Come, sit here.” But he said to him, “Who is it?” And he sat beside him.
He chose ten men from the elders of the town and seated them beside him.
He said to the relative with the right of redemption, “Naomi has sold me the portion of the field belonging to our brother Elimelech.”

“I said that I would disclose this and let you know, and tell you to buy it before these people sitting here. I myself have come forward to speak and to buy it before these elders of my people who are sitting here. Now, if you will redeem it, redeem it. But if you will not redeem it, tell me, so that I may know that you will not act as redeemer, and I will redeem it.” He said, “I will redeem it.”
Boaz said, “On the day you buy the field from Naomi and from Ruth the Moabite, the wife of the man who died, acquire it so that you may preserve the dead man’s name on his inheritance.”
The redeemer said, “I cannot redeem it, lest I ruin my own inheritance. You redeem it, because of my own lack of faithfulness, since I cannot redeem it.”

Now this was formerly the practice of redemption among the Israelites: to confirm a transfer of redemption rights, a man would take off his sandal and give it to his companion. This served as testimony in Israel.
The relative with the right of redemption said to Boaz, “Buy it for yourself.” And he took the sandal off his feet.
Boaz said to the elders and all the people, “You are witnesses today that I have bought from Naomi everything that belonged to Elimelech and everything that belonged to Mahlon and Chilion.

“And you, Ruth the Moabite, Mahlon’s wife, I have taken as my wife, to preserve the dead man’s name on his inheritance, so that the dead man’s name will not be forgotten, and the dead man’s memory will not be forgotten among his brothers and his clan. You are witnesses today.”

The elders and all the people at the village gate answered, “We are witnesses.” They blessed him and said to him, “May the Lord make this woman before you like Rachel and Leah, the two who built a household for Israel. Do mighty deeds in Ephrathah, and call it Bethlehem.
“May your household be like the household of Perez, whom Tamar bore to Judah. May the Lord give you offspring by this woman.”
Boaz took Ruth, and she became his wife. He slept with her, and the Lord gave to him, and she conceived and bore a son.
The women said to Naomi, “Blessed is the Lord, who has not taken away the redeemer today. You will proclaim his name in Israel.
“He will be a comfort to your soul and a provider for your town, because your daughter-in-law, who loves you, has borne him—she who is better in your eyes than seven sons.”
Naomi took the child, laid him in her lap, and became his caregiver.
Her neighbor said, “A son has been born to Naomi,” and named him Obed. He was the father of Jesse, the father of David.
These are the descendants of Perez: Perez was the father of Hezron.
Hezron was the father of Ram. Ram was the father of Amminadab.
Amminadab was the father of Nahshon. Nahshon was the father of Salmon.
Salmon was the father of Boaz. Boaz was the father of Obed.
Obed was the father of Jesse. Jesse was the father of King David. The book of Ruth is finished.
